explanations.answer: I am more righteous than God
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Elihu, the younger man who waited to speak, asks Job, "Do you think this is just? You say, 'I am more righteous than God.'" (Job 35:2) Those are Elihu's words about Job, and he's putting them right on the table. I think that's a pretty heavy thing to say to a man who's hurting.

explanations.answer: I am wiser than my friends
explanations.explanation: Close, because Elihu does talk about Job's friends, but not here. In Job 35:2 the claim Elihu quotes is "I am more righteous than God." Friend, I once picked the wrong box size three batches in a row, so I know the feeling of grabbing the nearest answer. Wisdom comes up later in this passage, but the claim itself is about righteousness.

explanations.answer: I am stronger than my troubles
explanations.explanation: That one sounds like something a tough guy would say, but it isn't what Elihu quotes. He says Job claims, "I am more righteous than God." (Job 35:2) Strength never comes up in that verse at all. I'd have loved to see a stamper claim he's stronger than his troubles, because mine came with dust bunnies.

explanations.answer: Does doing right even pay off
explanations.explanation: Yep. Elihu quotes Job asking, "What does it profit me, and what benefit do I gain apart from sin?" (Job 35:3) Profit and benefit are money words, so the question underneath is whether doing right pays off. That's what Elihu hears in it, and he's about to answer.

explanations.answer: Why are my friends so harsh
explanations.explanation: Job's friends do come up in this passage, since Elihu says his reply is for them too (Job 35:4). But the question Elihu quotes in verse 3 is about profit and benefit. Nobody's being called harsh there. Think of it like asking a cookie box what's in it for the cookies. It's a payoff question.

I get why you'd pick it, since Job is hurting and waiting is the whole mood of this book. But Elihu quotes something else: "What does it profit me, and what benefit do I gain apart from sin?" (Job 35:3) That's about what doing right gets you. A question about when it ends would sound a lot different.

Right on. Elihu says, "I will reply to you and to your friends as well." (Job 35:4) So Job isn't the only one getting an answer. His three friends are sitting right there too. That's a full kitchen, and everybody's getting a plate.

Job's wife does show up earlier in the book (Job 2:9), but she's not in this verse. Elihu says, "I will reply to you and to your friends as well." (Job 35:4) So the answer is friends. Nobody's wife is getting a reply here.

Job did have servants earlier in the story (Job 1:15), but Elihu isn't talking to them here. He says, "I will reply to you and to your friends as well." (Job 35:4) The friends are the ones sitting in on this. The servants are off doing other things.

That's it. Elihu says, "If you sin, what do you accomplish against Him? If you multiply your transgressions, what do you do to Him?" (Job 35:6) After pointing Job at the clouds high above him, Elihu is saying sin doesn't touch God. I think the sky is there to show how high up God is.

Clouds do make you think of storms, I'll give you that. But Elihu never mentions a storm here. He asks, "If you sin, what do you accomplish against Him?" (Job 35:6) The point is that sin doesn't do anything to God. Friend, I once checked the forecast for a whole batch and it was an indoor oven.

Nope, Elihu isn't saying God can't see it. He asks, "If you sin, what do you accomplish against Him?" (Job 35:6) That's a question about what the sin does to God, and the answer he's pointing at is nothing. Hiding doesn't come up in the verse.

Yes! Elihu says, "Your wickedness affects only a man like yourself, and your righteousness only a son of man." (Job 35:8) He's saying it lands on people, not on God. Same goes for the good stuff. A person is the one who feels it.

Not quite. Elihu says, "Your wickedness affects only a man like yourself, and your righteousness only a son of man." (Job 35:8) He says a man like yourself. He isn't talking about a king. I think that's a good reminder that most of us are just regular folks, even those of us in tall white hats.

Priests don't come up in this verse. Elihu says, "Your wickedness affects only a man like yourself, and your righteousness only a son of man." (Job 35:8) The word he uses is man, plain and simple. It's all about Job and people like him.

Yes, that's the one. Elihu says no one asks, "Where is God my Maker, who gives us songs in the night…" (Job 35:10) So in his telling, people cry out about the oppression but skip asking about God. That's how Elihu puts it, and I'll let his words stand.

That sounds like a natural thing to ask when you're under oppression, but it's not the question Elihu names. He says no one asks, "Where is God my Maker, who gives us songs in the night…" (Job 35:10) The missing question is about God as Maker. Punishing the mighty isn't in the verse.

Waiting is a big theme in this book, so I see why you'd pick it. But Elihu says no one asks, "Where is God my Maker, who gives us songs in the night…" (Job 35:10) That's the question he says is missing. How long isn't mentioned in verse 10.

Right. Elihu says, "There they cry out, but He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men." (Job 35:12) That's what he says, and he gives a reason in the same breath. Remember, these are Elihu's words, and he's talking about people crying out under oppression.

This one is true, so the text does say it. Elihu says, "There they cry out, but He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men." (Job 35:12) He says God does not answer them. The reason he gives comes right after, in the same verse.

explanations.answer: Because of the pride of evil men
explanations.explanation: Yes. Elihu says, "There they cry out, but He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men." (Job 35:12) That's the reason he gives, word for word. It's his explanation, so I'll stay right inside what he said.

explanations.answer: Because of the sins of their fathers
explanations.explanation: That's not in this verse. Elihu says God does not answer "because of the pride of evil men." (Job 35:12) Nothing about fathers shows up there. It's a good reminder to stick to what the text says, not what sounds like it fits.

explanations.answer: Because of the fear in their hearts
explanations.explanation: Fear sounds like it could fit, but Elihu doesn't say it. His words are, "There they cry out, but He does not answer, because of the pride of evil men." (Job 35:12) The reason he gives is pride, and it belongs to evil men. Nobody's heart is mentioned.
That's right. Elihu says, "Surely God does not listen to empty pleas, and the Almighty does not take note of it." (Job 35:13) Listen is the first blank. It goes together with empty in the second one.
Yes, empty is the word. Elihu says, "Surely God does not listen to empty pleas…" (Job 35:13) That's his phrase for the kind of pleas he means. Pair it with listen and the sentence is whole.

Singing does show up earlier, when Elihu mentions "songs in the night" (Job 35:10). But verse 13 says, "Surely God does not listen to empty pleas." Sing doesn't fit the blank. Friend, I'd sing it if it did.

Honest feels like a fair word to put there, but Elihu doesn't use it. He says, "Surely God does not listen to empty pleas, and the Almighty does not take note of it." (Job 35:13) The word that fits the second blank is empty. Honest isn't in the verse.
I get it, I'm the loud one in this bakery. But Elihu doesn't say loud pleas. He says, "Surely God does not listen to empty pleas." (Job 35:13) The words that fill the blanks are listen and empty.

Actually, it's the other way around. Elihu says, "How much less, then, when you say that you do not see Him, that your case is before Him and you must wait for Him…" (Job 35:14) How much less means less, not more. So Elihu isn't saying God will listen more.

Yes, that's the right call. Elihu says, "How much less, then, when you say that you do not see Him, that your case is before Him and you must wait for Him…" (Job 35:14) He says how much less. Elihu isn't saying God will listen to Job more.

Yep. Elihu finishes with, "So Job opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge." (Job 35:16) That's the last thing he says in this passage. I think it's a hard thing to hear when you're already hurting.

Comfort is a nice word, and Job could use some. But Elihu says, "So Job opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge." (Job 35:16) The blank is knowledge. Comfort isn't in the verse.

Kindness would have been sweet, but that's not what Elihu says. His words are, "So Job opens his mouth in vain and multiplies words without knowledge." (Job 35:16) The word that fits is knowledge. Kindness doesn't show up in the verse.
